en.statement: A Git blob stores the file's name as metadata alongside its contents.
en.explanation: A blob contains file data, not a filename field.

en.statement: A Git tree represents a subdirectory by referring to another tree object's ID.
en.explanation: A directory tree links to subtree objects instead of embedding their full structures.

en.statement: A Git commit identifies its project's snapshot through a top-level tree ID.
en.explanation: The commit points to the tree representing the complete recorded project state.

en.statement: Git uses a single identity field for both author and committer in a commit.
en.explanation: A commit has separate author and committer fields, including their respective timestamps.

en.statement: Git includes tag alongside commit, tree and blob as a core object type.
en.explanation: Tag is a distinct object type, rather than an extra field added to a commit object.

en.statement: Git uses an object's type as part of the input that determines its ID.
en.explanation: Git hashes an object's type together with its content when calculating its identity.

en.statement: Git edits an existing blob in place when a tracked file changes.
en.explanation: Stored objects are immutable; recording different content involves a different object.

en.statement: Git duplicates an unchanged file's blob when another file changes in a new commit.
en.explanation: Git reuses the existing blob ID for a file whose contents stay the same.

en.statement: In Git 2.56, git init uses sha1 as its built-in default object format.
en.explanation: Git 2.56 defaults to sha1 for new repositories; --object-format selects another enabled format.

en.statement: Git stores a commit's tree and blobs together in one loose object file.
en.explanation: Git stores a loose object in its own file, rather than grouping a commit with its referenced objects.

en.statement: Git stores some related object versions as deltas inside packfiles.
en.explanation: Within a packfile, Git can represent an object using another object plus differences, reducing duplicated data.

en.statement: On a branch, HEAD holds refs/heads/<branch> rather than a commit ID.
en.explanation: gitglossary calls HEAD the prime example of a symref: it holds ref: refs/heads/<branch>, and Git dereferences it to that branch, which holds the commit ID.

en.statement: With detached HEAD, a new commit advances the previously checked-out branch.
en.explanation: Committing while detached moves HEAD to the new commit; existing branch tips stay unchanged.

en.statement: gitglossary describes pseudorefs as refs that git update-ref treats as read-only.
en.explanation: gitglossary lists FETCH_HEAD and MERGE_HEAD as pseudorefs: refs with different semantics from normal refs, readable through ordinary Git commands but not writable with git update-ref.

en.statement: In revision syntax, M^2 follows two first-parent links from merge commit M.
en.explanation: For a merge commit M, M^2 selects the second parent; M~2 follows the first parent twice.

en.statement: In Git's revision syntax, @ resolves to the same commit as the HEAD reference.
en.explanation: The @ shorthand substitutes for HEAD in revision notation.

en.statement: Git accepts @{-1} for the branch or commit visited before the current checkout.
en.explanation: @{-1} follows checkout history, making it useful for returning to the previous checkout.

en.statement: For divergent tips A and B, git log A...B selects history unique to either side.
en.explanation: In git log, A...B includes commits reachable from A or B and excludes commits reachable from both.

en.statement: Git resolves HEAD:README.md by looking up README.md in the index.
en.explanation: HEAD:README.md identifies that path in the tree recorded by HEAD.

en.statement: In revision arguments, branch release takes precedence over a tag named release.
en.explanation: Git resolves an ambiguous short ref name by checking tags before branches.

en.statement: After git add stages a file, later edits to that file enter the staged version.
en.explanation: git add captures content at invocation time. Further edits need another staging operation.

en.statement: A plain git commit builds its new snapshot from the contents prepared in the index.
en.explanation: The index supplies the proposed project state for a commit made with no content-selection options or paths.

en.statement: git diff by itself shows the changes staged for the next commit.
en.explanation: On its own, git diff compares the working tree with the index, showing unstaged changes.

en.statement: git commit -a includes a newly created file that Git still lists as untracked.
en.explanation: git commit -a stages tracked modifications and deletions; an untracked new file needs to be added first.

en.statement: git rm --cached leaves the removed path's working-tree file in place.
en.explanation: git rm --cached removes the index entry while retaining the local file.

en.statement: Adding a tracked file's path to .gitignore removes that file from the index.
en.explanation: .gitignore governs untracked paths; matching an existing tracked file leaves its tracked status unchanged.

en.statement: In a root .gitignore, doc/output.log also matches nested/doc/output.log.
en.explanation: In a root .gitignore, the slash in doc/output.log makes the pattern relative to the repository root.

en.statement: In .gitignore, src/**/test.js matches src/test.js as well as deeper matching paths.
en.explanation: In .gitignore, /**/ matches zero or more directory levels.

en.statement: A later !build/keep.txt rule re-includes the file while build/ keeps its parent directory excluded.
en.explanation: In .gitignore, an excluded parent blocks re-inclusion of files beneath it, even with a later negated pattern.

en.statement: A repository's .gitignore rules outrank conflicting patterns in core.excludesFile.
en.explanation: Patterns in .gitignore take priority over the global exclusion file specified by core.excludesFile.

en.statement: git check-ignore -v identifies the ignore rule responsible for excluding a path.
en.explanation: git check-ignore -v reports the matching pattern and its source, helping diagnose why a path is ignored.

en.statement: After git branch topic, HEAD points to the newly created topic branch.
en.explanation: git branch topic creates the branch reference while leaving the active branch unchanged.

en.statement: git switch -c makes creation of the new branch conditional on a successful switch.
en.explanation: If the switch fails, git switch -c leaves the proposed new branch uncreated.

en.statement: git switch <branch> discards local edits that conflict with the destination branch's files.
en.explanation: git switch refuses an ordinary switch that would lose local changes.

en.statement: git switch --merge adds a merge commit containing local edits to the destination branch's history.
en.explanation: git switch --merge carries local edits across the switch by saving and reapplying them; they remain uncommitted.

en.statement: With --guess, git switch creates a missing local branch from a uniquely matching remote-tracking branch.
en.explanation: git switch --guess uses the uniquely matching remote-tracking branch as the new branch's starting point and upstream.

en.statement: git checkout serves both branch switching and restoration of selected working-tree files.
en.explanation: git checkout interprets branch arguments as branch switches and path arguments as requests to restore files.

en.statement: git branch -d judges an upstream-tracking branch's merged status against HEAD.
en.explanation: git branch -d checks the configured upstream; it uses HEAD when the branch has no upstream.

en.statement: git branch -m carries the branch's reflog and its branch.<name> settings over to the new name.
en.explanation: Renaming moves the branch's configuration, such as its upstream, and renames its reflog, adding an entry that records the rename. The commits themselves are untouched.

en.statement: git branch --merged lists branches according to whether their file contents match the current branch.
en.explanation: git branch --merged selects branches whose tips are reachable from HEAD, rather than comparing file contents.

en.statement: In Git 2.56, an unconfigured git init chooses main as its default initial branch name.
en.explanation: Git 2.56 defaults to master for git init. init.defaultBranch or --initial-branch overrides that choice.

en.statement: A fast-forward merge moves the current branch tip to the existing commit at the incoming branch tip.
en.explanation: Git integrates a fast-forward by advancing the current branch reference, rather than creating a merge commit.

en.statement: git merge --squash prepares the next commit to record the incoming branch tip as an additional parent.
en.explanation: git merge --squash omits MERGE_HEAD, so the subsequent commit does not record the incoming branch as a merge parent.

en.statement: In Git 2.56, git merge selects ort by default when integrating a single other branch.
en.explanation: Git 2.56 uses ort for the ordinary two-head case unless a strategy override selects something else.

en.statement: In Git 2.56, choosing recursive selects a different merge implementation from ort.
en.explanation: Git 2.56 treats recursive as another name for ort, not as a separate implementation.

en.statement: git merge -X ours discards incoming edits even in text regions that merge cleanly.
en.explanation: git merge -X ours favors our conflicting hunks but retains clean incoming edits; the ours strategy discards incoming content.

en.statement: Git's octopus strategy can handle a complex multi-branch merge that requires manual conflict resolution.
en.explanation: The octopus strategy refuses complex merges needing manual resolution; it is intended for combining compatible branch heads.

en.statement: With merge.conflictStyle set to diff3, Git includes the base text inside a textual conflict.
en.explanation: The diff3 conflict style shows the original text alongside both competing versions, giving context for their edits.

en.statement: In a merge conflict, Git uses index stage 2 for HEAD's version of the conflicted path.
en.explanation: Merge index stages represent the base at 1, HEAD at 2 and MERGE_HEAD at 3, when those versions exist.

en.statement: Deleting a file's conflict markers in your editor marks that path as resolved in Git's index.
en.explanation: After editing a conflicted file, run git add on that path to mark its resolution in the index.

source.title: Pro Git, 2nd ed., 3.2: Basic Branching and Merging

en.statement: git merge --abort can fail to reconstruct local edits that were uncommitted when the merge began.
en.explanation: git merge --abort attempts recovery, but pre-existing local edits can prevent complete restoration.

en.statement: With standard settings, git rebase keeps commits whose patches already appear in upstream.
en.explanation: Ordinary rebase drops clean upstream cherry-picks; --reapply-cherry-picks changes that selection.

en.statement: git rebase --onto transplants a selected segment of a branch onto a separately chosen base.
en.explanation: git rebase --onto separates the new base from the upstream boundary that selects the topic commits to replay.

en.statement: In Git 2.56, an unconfigured git rebase uses the apply backend by default.
en.explanation: Git 2.56 defaults to the merge backend, including for non-interactive rebases.

en.statement: By default, git rebase linearizes the replayed range, leaving its merge commits out of the new history.
en.explanation: Rebase drops merge commits from the todo list unless --rebase-merges or rebase.rebaseMerges asks it to recreate them; manual resolutions in those merges must then be redone.

en.statement: In an interactive rebase, a plain fixup entry combines its message with the preceding commit's message.
en.explanation: A plain fixup entry folds its changes into the preceding commit while discarding the fixup commit's message.

en.statement: git rebase --autosquash moves recognized fixup! commits beside the commits they modify in the todo list.
en.explanation: Autosquash matches commit markers to targets and schedules the marked commits immediately after those targets.

en.statement: git rebase --update-refs moves affected branch tips even when another worktree has those branches checked out.
en.explanation: git rebase --update-refs excludes other branches checked out in worktrees from its additional branch updates.

en.statement: During a rebase conflict, ours identifies the original topic-branch changes currently being replayed.
en.explanation: During rebase, ours is the new base plus the changes replayed so far; theirs is the topic-side version being applied.

en.statement: Pro Git advises preserving shared commits when other developers may have based work on them.
en.explanation: Pro Git warns against rebasing commits shared outside your repository when others may depend on that history.

en.statement: git reset --soft replaces the index with the snapshot at the destination commit.
en.explanation: git reset --soft leaves the index contents unchanged while moving the branch tip.

en.statement: From a clean checkout, git reset --mixed HEAD~1 leaves edits to files tracked in both commits unstaged.
en.explanation: A mixed reset makes the index match the selected commit but keeps working files, leaving their differences unstaged.

en.statement: git reset --hard can overwrite untracked files that obstruct restoring the selected commit.
en.explanation: A hard reset restores the target tree even when untracked files obstruct it; those files are not protected.

en.statement: git reset with a pathspec changes selected index entries while leaving the branch tip in place.
en.explanation: A pathspec reset copies the chosen paths into the index; it preserves the working files and the branch position.

en.statement: When undoing a merge, git reset --merge discards unrelated edits left unstaged before that merge.
en.explanation: git reset --merge preserves unrelated unstaged edits when rolling back a merge.

en.statement: git reset --keep proceeds when a locally edited file also differs between HEAD and the target.
en.explanation: git reset --keep aborts when a file that it would update between HEAD and the target also has local changes.

en.statement: Plain git restore takes a tracked file's replacement content from the current HEAD commit.
en.explanation: git restore defaults to the index for working-tree restoration; adding --staged changes the default source to HEAD.

en.statement: git restore --source can rewind the current branch to the commit supplying the file contents.
en.explanation: git restore changes file contents, not the branch position; selecting an older source does not rewind history.

source.title: Git Reference: git (Reset, restore and revert)

en.statement: git revert records an inverse change as a new commit after the existing history.
en.explanation: git revert adds a commit reversing an earlier change while preserving the commits already in history.

source.title: Git Reference: git (Reset, restore and revert)

en.statement: The git-revert manual requires a clean working tree for the usual commit-producing form.
en.explanation: git-revert documents a clean starting state for its normal operation: tracked content matches HEAD.

en.statement: Reverting a merge makes a later merge of the same branch replay the changes that the first merge introduced.
en.explanation: A merge revert retains ancestry. Later merges bring changes from commits outside the reverted merge's ancestry, rather than replaying its old changes.

en.statement: A branch's reflog retains earlier tip values after operations that rewrite its history.
en.explanation: A reflog records reference updates, so previous branch positions remain available while the entries are retained.

en.statement: Git's HEAD reflog includes branch switches alongside movements caused by new commits.
en.explanation: The HEAD reflog records checkout transitions even when a switch leaves both branch tips unchanged.

en.statement: HEAD@{1} follows the current commit's first-parent link when Git resolves that revision.
en.explanation: HEAD@{1} selects HEAD's previous recorded value; one reference update can jump across several commits.

en.statement: git push automatically transfers a branch's reflog along with that branch's reachable commits.
en.explanation: Reflog entries stay in the repository where they are recorded; pushing a branch does not transfer its reflog.

en.statement: git reflog expire removes the commit objects associated with the entries it expires.
en.explanation: git reflog expire removes selected log entries; expiring an entry is distinct from pruning its commit object.

en.statement: Before a whole-branch reset, Git saves the branch's old tip in ORIG_HEAD for that operation.
en.explanation: ORIG_HEAD records the pre-reset tip as a recovery point. A later operation may replace that saved value.

en.statement: Git deletes detached commits immediately when a branch switch leaves them outside branch history.
en.explanation: Detached commits remain after switching away; deletion is eventual and depends on garbage collection and retained references.

en.statement: Git's garbage collector can retain contents referenced by the index even before they enter a commit.
en.explanation: git gc protects objects referenced by the index, so staged content need not already belong to a commit.

en.statement: Git classifies an unreachable parent as dangling even while another existing commit names it as a parent.
en.explanation: A dangling commit lacks references from other objects. An unreachable parent can still have an unreachable child referring to it.

en.statement: Creating a branch at a dangling commit found by git fsck makes that recovered history reachable again.
en.explanation: Use the recovered commit ID as a new branch's starting point to retain that commit and its ancestors.

source.title: Pro Git, 2nd ed., 10.7: Maintenance and Data Recovery

en.statement: By default, git stash push saves staged and unstaged changes to tracked files.
en.explanation: A normal stash captures tracked edits from the index and working tree so you can resume that work later.

source.title: Pro Git, 2nd ed., 7.3: Stashing and Cleaning

en.statement: git stash push -u includes files excluded by ignore rules in the saved stash entry.
en.explanation: git stash push -u adds untracked files; use -a to include ignored files as well.

source.title: Pro Git, 2nd ed., 7.3: Stashing and Cleaning

en.statement: git stash push --keep-index leaves staged changes ready for a commit.
en.explanation: The --keep-index option leaves existing staged changes intact, enabling tests of the staged work in isolation.

source.title: Pro Git, 2nd ed., 7.3: Stashing and Cleaning

en.statement: git stash pop removes the saved entry when applying it produces conflicts.
en.explanation: When git stash pop encounters conflicts, it retains the stash entry for later use.

en.statement: git stash branch starts its new branch at the current tip of the stash's original branch.
en.explanation: git stash branch starts at the commit that was HEAD when the stash was created, avoiding conflicts from later branch changes.

en.statement: git fsck can locate a dropped stash entry whose commit objects remain in the repository.
en.explanation: git fsck --unreachable can help identify a dropped stash's surviving commit for recovery.

en.statement: Linked worktrees reuse the same repository object database.
en.explanation: Objects created in one worktree are available to the other worktrees attached to that repository.

en.statement: Staging a file in a linked worktree updates the main worktree's index.
en.explanation: Linked worktrees keep separate indexes, so their staged contents are independent.

en.statement: git worktree add <path> <branch> can take a branch already checked out in another worktree.
en.explanation: git worktree add refuses an occupied branch by default; --force overrides that safeguard.

en.statement: git worktree lock preserves a linked worktree's metadata while its storage is disconnected.
en.explanation: Locking protects worktree metadata from pruning when a portable drive or network share is temporarily unavailable.

en.statement: git cherry-pick replaces the current tree with the source commit's complete snapshot.
en.explanation: git cherry-pick reapplies the change a commit introduced, preserving unrelated destination-branch content.

source.title: Pro Git, 2nd ed., 5.3: Maintaining a Project

en.statement: git cherry-pick -n applies changes to both the index and working tree for later committing.
en.explanation: The -n option leaves applied changes uncommitted, letting you combine or adjust them before committing.

en.statement: For a merge commit, git cherry-pick -m chooses the parent used as the change's baseline.
en.explanation: git cherry-pick -m replays the merge's difference from the selected parent.

en.statement: git-cherry-pick suggests -x for recording a backport between two publicly visible branches.
en.explanation: For a conflict-free cherry-pick, -x adds the source commit ID to the message, helping readers trace a publicly shared backport.

en.statement: git cherry-pick --skip can roll back the commits already applied earlier in the same sequence.
en.explanation: git cherry-pick --skip omits the current commit and proceeds; --abort restores the pre-sequence state.

en.statement: By default, git cherry-pick may drop a commit that becomes empty because its changes already exist.
en.explanation: The default cherry-pick stops when an originally nonempty commit becomes empty, leaving you to decide how to handle it.

en.statement: git bisect reserves its classification labels for the fixed pair good and bad.
en.explanation: git bisect accepts old/new or custom terms to locate changes such as performance improvements.

en.statement: git bisect skip can leave several commits as candidates for the first bad change.
en.explanation: Skipping a commit beside the regression boundary can leave Git unable to identify one exact culprit.

en.statement: git bisect run can classify a test script's exit code 125 as evidence that the commit is bad.
en.explanation: git bisect run reads 125 as skip, 0 as good, and 1 through 127 except 125 as bad; other codes abort the search.

en.statement: git bisect reset chooses the first bad commit as its default return destination.
en.explanation: git bisect reset returns to the checkout from before git bisect start when you provide no destination.

source.title: Pro Git, 2nd ed., 7.10: Debugging with Git

en.statement: git bisect start --first-parent can identify the merge that brings a regression onto the main line.
en.explanation: Following first parents attributes an integrated regression to the merge instead of a commit inside the merged branch.

en.statement: A remote-tracking branch records Git's last known position of a remote branch.
en.explanation: A remote-tracking ref is a local bookmark updated by communication with the remote, rather than a live view.

en.statement: Git requires the clone's source remote to keep the name origin for later fetches.
en.explanation: origin is a conventional default name. Git accepts another name for the same remote.

en.statement: With its standard refspec, git fetch origin moves the current branch to the fetched tip.
en.explanation: The standard fetch mapping updates refs/remotes/origin/*, leaving the local branch and working tree for a later integration step.

en.statement: git fetch --prune can remove tracking refs for branches deleted from a normally configured remote.
en.explanation: With the usual branch refspec, --prune clears stale tracking refs. fetch.prune enables this cleanup during routine fetches.

en.statement: git branch -u sends the local branch's commits to the newly selected upstream.
en.explanation: git branch -u changes local tracking configuration; it leaves publishing the branch to a separate operation.

en.statement: In Git 2.56, an unconfigured git pull resolves divergent histories by creating a merge commit.
en.explanation: Unconfigured Git 2.56 uses --ff-only for pull, refusing divergent history until you choose an integration method.

en.statement: Using push.default=simple, git push selects a differently named upstream on the upstream remote.
en.explanation: When pushing to the upstream remote, simple requires the local branch and its upstream to share a name.

en.statement: An ordinary git push to an existing branch requires the remote tip to be an ancestor of the new tip.
en.explanation: The normal branch update rule requires a fast-forward, preserving the remote branch's existing ancestry.

en.statement: git push origin :topic, with its empty source, deletes the branch topic on the remote.
en.explanation: A refspec with an empty <src> deletes the <dst> ref from the remote repository, the same as git push --delete origin topic.

en.statement: An annotated tag takes its tagger identity and creation date from the tagged commit.
en.explanation: An annotated tag object records its own tagger identity, tagging date and message.

en.statement: When creating a tag, supplying its message with git tag -m implicitly selects an annotated tag.
en.explanation: git tag -m implies -a when you supply a message and leave the tag-type flags unspecified.

en.statement: By default, git describe can select a lightweight tag to name a commit.
en.explanation: git describe normally selects annotated tags; --tags extends its search to lightweight tags.

en.statement: A lightweight tag can label a directory snapshot by pointing directly to a tree object.
en.explanation: A lightweight tag names a Git object directly; the target need not be a commit.

en.statement: By default, git push transfers local tags that mark the branch being pushed.
en.explanation: A normal branch push leaves local tags unpublished; tag refs need an explicit push selection or tag-pushing option.

en.statement: git push --follow-tags automatically selects missing lightweight tags reachable from the pushed branch.
en.explanation: git push --follow-tags adds missing reachable annotated tags; --tags selects tags regardless of annotation or reachability.

en.statement: By default, git fetch also retrieves tags that point into the history it fetches.
en.explanation: Git follows tags pointing into fetched history unless tag options or remote configuration override that behavior.

en.statement: The git tag manual recommends reusing a published tag name with git tag -f after correcting its target.
en.explanation: The git tag manual recommends a new name once others have seen a tag, calling reuse with git tag -f the 'insane thing'.

en.statement: git tag -d can delete a named tag from the configured remote repository.
en.explanation: git tag -d removes a local tag. Use git push --delete with an explicit remote tag ref to delete its remote counterpart.

en.statement: Plain git checkout enters detached HEAD when you select an unambiguous tag pointing to a commit.
en.explanation: A tag checkout selects the tagged commit for inspection rather than attaching HEAD to a branch.

en.statement: git merge --ff v1.2^0 can fast-forward to the commit behind an annotated v1.2 tag.
en.explanation: v1.2^0 peels the annotated tag to the commit it points to, so git merge sees a plain commit and fast-forwards when the current tip is its ancestor. git-merge suggests ^0 to catch up to a tagged release.
